      Surface roughness analysis: A comprehensive review of measurement techniques, methodologies, and modeling

      K. Sushil https://orcid.org/0009-0008-7862-7133, J. Ramkumar, and C. Chandraprakash https://orcid.org/0000-0002-5222-0932 chindamc@iitk.ac.inView all authors and affiliations

      Abstract

      The scale and value of surface roughness affect the wetting, fatigue, damping, emissivity, heat transfer, and aesthetic characteristics leading to applications in food, chemical, medical, and traditional mechanical industries. Starting with the definitions of roughness parameters, in this work, we presented a comprehensive review of various aspects required to characterize surface roughness. Subsequently, a well-arranged literature survey on the use of several roughness-sensing methods for various machining processes was presented. In tandem, the theoretical aspects of sensing and their limits on resolution, sensitivity, range, and accuracy have been described. Thereafter, mathematical models to reconstruct surface profiles were outlined. We also presented the ways for online measurements of roughness and integration of the former with the standards of Industry 4.0. With details on all aspects of roughness, this work is expected to assist the researchers and engineers in the selection of appropriate roughness measurement techniques that lead to application in various industries.

      Introduction

      In all additive and traditional manufacturing processes, both roughness and waviness are inevitable parameters of any workpiece at different length scales. Roughness affects the optical,1 tribological,2 damping,3 thermal,4 wetting,5 fluid flow,6 biomedical,7 and catalytic8 properties of surfaces. The magnitude of the roughness of surfaces also has implications in biological applications such as in the growth of fibroblasts,9 biofouling,10 and protection of cells from shear forces.11 Thus, roughness plays a crucial role in deciding the performance and long-term usability of the workpiece. In the year 2011, “surface roughness” was defined per the standard BS 113412 as “the pattern or texture of surface irregularities that are inherent in the production process, excluding waviness and errors of formation.”13
      The vertical undulations of the surface are the key features in the quantification of roughness apart from the lateral dimensions of the surface profile. For example, scratches have depths of a few tenths of a micrometer and widths of up to a few micrometers.14 Whereas thin films used in optics have heights and lateral dimensions in nanometers.15 Further, thin films with pancake-like structures on the surface have roughness on the order of microscale.16 Roughness quantifies the surface topography over a millimeter scale, while waviness corresponds to variations over a larger length scale. For example, the maximum peak-to-valley amplitude could be 100 nm with a maximum lateral size of 106 nm. Roughnesses of commercially polished optical elements such as lenses, mirror substrates, windows, filters, beam splitters, etc. have a root-mean-square (RMS) roughness value in the range 1.5−2.5 nm. While super-polished optical elements have RMS roughness < 0.5 nm RMS, the finest polished surfaces have an RMS roughness < 0.1 nm. A typical machined surface can have RMS roughness ranging between 10 nm and 1 µm or more, based on the manufacturing process used. The range of average roughness achieved by different manufacturing processes is shown in Figure 1.
      To have a successful translation of roughness measurement to the standards of Industry 4.0, a proper understanding of the machining process31 and the selection of sensors based on the process and their parameters are crucial steps. Accordingly, in this review, we present a comprehensive summary of the roughness with a focus on definitions, instruments, physics, analysis of quantifying roughness, and the way forward for Industry 4.0 in surface roughness. The following aspects of roughness are addressed: (a) the detailed nomenclature of the roughness parameters used in two- and three-dimensions are presented in the first section; (b) the summary of the use of different roughness measurement sensors such as profilometer, ultrasonic transducer, laser, fiber optics, etc. in various machining and polishing processes are detailed in the second section; (c) the mathematical functions used for representing roughness are discussed in the third section; and (d) the efforts needed to integrate the methods of roughness measurement for Industry 4.0 are outlined in the fourth section. The detailed analysis presented in this work will help in the selection and understanding of the appropriate roughness measurement technique for various machining and polishing processes.

      Surface roughness parameters

      In general, while the surface roughness is mostly quantified in terms of the local or relative average of peaks, these do not fully account for the spatial distribution of the peaks and length scales. Surface metrology is about profile measurements and quantification. Among many standards, the ISO 21920-232 describes the main profile parameters. The application of parameters and selection of cutoff length are explained in ISO 21920-3.33 ISO 16610-2134 describes the Gaussian profile filter for filtration of profiles. ISO 16610-6235 specifies the characteristics of a linear areal spline filter. ISO 21920-232 describes the filtering and height characterization using the curves of linear material ratio and material probability. Most of these standards were established or last amended in the late 1990s. ISO 2517836 and ISO 2192037 are the latest standards for surface texture, focusing on areal surface texture. Starting from the widely used average roughness Ra and root-mean-squared roughness Rq, many parameters have been defined to quantify roughness.
      Roughness is characterized either in two- (2D) or three-dimensions (3D). Measurements in 2D are simpler and provide a good estimate of the nature of the surface for simple machining processes such as those done on lathe and milling machines. As 2D measurements are robust and provide a faster estimate of roughness, these have been extensively used in the past few decades. However, with the advent of sophisticated, advanced machining and polishing processes suitable for complex shaped objects, emphasis has increased on 3D characterization of the surface topography. Recent literature also highlights the need for 3D measurements for different applications.38-40 A summary of the classification of parameters to quantify 2D and 3D measurements of roughness is given in Table 1. Although widely used, the list is not exhaustive. Per the ISO 21920 several other parameters which are a combination of the parameters discussed so far are used: (a) Functional parameters Rk, Rpk, Rvk which represent the core height, reduced peak height, and reduced valley depth, respectively; (b) Volume parameters: Per ISO 25178 − 2, Rvmp, Rvmc, Rvv, Rvvc, and Rvvv represent the volumes of the reduced peaks, core material, void, core void, and valley void, respectively; and (c) Motifs parameters: ISO 25178−2, defines the density of peaks Rpd, mean curvature of peaks Rpd, mean height of the five highest peaks R5p, and mean depth of the five deepest valleys R5v. Additionally, some parameters Rhhm, Rhhq, and Rhhx are calculated on hills which represent the mean, standard deviation, and maximum of their height. Similarly, Rhwm, Rhwq, and Rhwx represent their width, and Rhvm, Rhvq, and Rhvx represent their volume. The definition and mathematical representation of the most commonly used height and peak-to-valley parameters are described. The emphasis is laid on the definitions, applicability, and limitations wherever possible.

      Arithmetic average height

      Arithmetic average height or center line average is defined as the mean of absolute deviations of the profile from a reference line over a sampling length ℓ. The reference line is chosen at the average of the measured heights. A 3D machined surface is shown in Figure 2(a). The roughness over a region 3ℓ × 3ℓ is shown in Figure 2(b). For this surface, the profile along a line is shown in Figure 2(c). The profiles z(x) and Z(x,y), also called the amplitude functions, are taken from the reference mean line in 2D and 3D, respectively. The arithmetic average heights in 2D and 3D, that is, Ra and Sa, respectively, are calculated as:
      𝓁𝓁Ra=1l∫0lz(x)dxand Sa=1A∬z(x,y)dxdy
      (1)
      where A represents the area of measurement of the profile and | · | indicates the absolute value of the arguments. In discrete form
      Ra=1n∑i=1nzxiand Sa=1mn∑j=1m∑k=1nzxj,yj
      (2)
      where m and n are the number of sampled points over ℓ.
      As Ra provides an adequate overall description of height fluctuations it is widely used for quality control. However, it does not provide any information about the shape, orientation, or frequency of the surface features. The limitation of Ra is the insensitiveness to slight changes in the profile, outliers or extreme values, making it unsuitable for characterizing surfaces with occasional extreme peaks or valleys.

      Root mean square roughness

      The root mean square or RMS roughness represents the standard deviation of surface irregularities over the sampling length ℓ. The RMS roughness in 2D and 3D, that is, Rq and Sq, respectively, are calculated as:
      𝓁𝓁Rq=1l∫0l[z(x)]2dx and Sq=1A∬[z(x,y)]2dxdy
      (3)
      In discrete form
      Rq=1n∑i=1n[z(x)]2andSq=1mn∑j=1m∑k=1nzxj,yj2
      (4)
      A rough 2D profile and the corresponding distribution of roughnesses are shown in Figure 2(a) and (b), respectively. For any sample, the normal distribution of the heights, Rq also represents its standard deviation.41 This is also shown in Figure 2(c). Together with Ra or Sa, Rq or Sq provide a unique representation of surface roughness. Rq is a more sensitive parameter than Ra toward peaks and valleys, as it accounts for the amplitudes of symmetric profiles.

      Maximum height of peaks

      It is defined as the maximum height of the profile above the reference mean line along each sampling length. Represented in 2D and 3D as Rp and Sp, respectively, the maximum height is defined as
      Rp=max[z(x)]and Sp=max[z(x,y)]
      (5)
      Rp for a 2D profile is shown in Figure 2(c). These parameters are important for moving parts such as those used in sliding. These parameters, Rp and Sp, primarily account for the protrusions and are useful in the compatibility of tolerances.

      Maximum depth of valleys

      It is defined as the maximum depth of the profile below the reference mean line along each sampling length. Represented in 2D and 3D as Rv and Sv, respectively, the maximum depth is defined as
      Rv=min[z(x)]andSv=min[Z(x,y)]
      (6)
      Rv for a 2D profile is shown in Figure 2(c). One main advantage of these two parameters is the quantification of deep scratches induced during abrasive machining or local tears.

      Mean height of peaks

      It is defined as the mean of maximum heights of peaks estimated over different sampling regions of identical lengths. Represented in 2D and 3D as Rpm and Spm, respectively, the mean height is given as
      Rpm=1mΣi=1mRpiand Spm=1mnΣj=1mΣk=1nSpkk
      (7)
      where Rpi and Spjk are the maximum height of peaks in the ith sampling region in 2D and sampling region at discrete location (j,k) in 3D.

      Mean depth of valleys

      It is defined as the mean of the maximum depth of valleys estimated over different sampling regions of identical lengths. Represented in 2D and 3D as Rvm and Svm, respectively, the mean depth is calculated as
      Rvm=1mΣi=1mRviandSvm=1mnΣj=1mΣk=1nSvjk
      (8)
      where Rvi and Svjk are the maximum height of valleys in the ith sampling region in 2D and sampling region at discrete location (j,k) in 3D, respectively. Per ISO 21920, the parameters {Rp, Rv, Rpm, Rvm} are now classified as peak-to-valley parameters rather than height parameters.

      Maximum height of the profile

      It is defined as the vertical distance from the highest peak to the lowest valley over different sampling regions of identical lengths. Represented in 2D and 3D are Rz and Sz, respectively, the maximum height is defined as
      Rz=Rp+Rx andSz=5p+Sx
      (9)
      These are important in applications such as sealing and the design of bearings, where a high tolerance is crucial.

      Skewness

      Surface skewness in 2D and 3D, indicated by Rsk and Ssk, respectively, are evaluated as42
      𝓁𝓁Rsk=1Rq31l∫0l[z(x)]3dxandSsk=1Sq31A∬[Z(x,y)]3dxdy
      (10)
      In discrete form
      Rsk=1Rq31nΣi=1nzxi3andSsk=1Sq31mnΣj=1mΣk=1nZxi,yj3
      (11)
      The skewness of the surface represents the symmetry of the local heights of the surface about the mean line. Surface skewness is the third central moment of profile amplitude function, whereas {Ra,Sa} and {Rq,Sq} are the first and second central moments of the amplitude function, respectively. Skewness is sensitive to the sparsely present deep valleys or high peaks. The general trend in peaks or valleys of the amplitude can be known based on the sign of the skewness. A symmetrical height profile, that is, a surface with as many peaks as valleys, has the value of skewness as zero. Profiles with less number of peaks but with deep valleys have negative skewness. Likewise, profiles with less number of valleys but with high peaks have positive skewness. The value of skewness depends on distribution of the material on the surface of the workpiece.
      Material distributions on the surfaces of positive skewness and negative skewness are shown in Figure 3(a) and (b), respectively. Surfaces of different shapes, but identical non-zero values of Ra, are distinguishable by the skewness parameters.

      Kurtosis

      Kurtosis in 2D and 3D, indicated by Rsk and Ssk, respectively, are evaluated as42
      𝓁𝓁Rku=1Rq41l∫0l[z(x)]4dxandSku=1sq41A∬[Z(x,y)]4dxdy
      (12)
      In discrete form
      Rsk=1Rq41nΣi=1nzxi3andSsk=1Sq41mnΣj=1mΣk=1nZxi,yj4
      (13)
      Kurtosis describes the sharpness of the surface profile. Mathematically, these are the fourth central moments of amplitude function over a sampling length or region. Essentially, {Rku,Sku} describe the difference between “broad and wavy” and “sharp and sudden” peaks or valleys. Surfaces with Rku > 3 are termed leptokurtic, that is, these profiles have many high peaks and a few low valleys. Similarly, surfaces with Rku < 3 are termed platykurtic, that is, these profiles have fewer high peaks and many low valleys. Examples of leptokurtic and platykurtic profiles are shown in Figure 4.
      Kurtosis and skewness are referred to in precision engineering. As most conventional machining processes lead to a near-normal distribution in the amplitudes of the surface profiles,43 these parameters are not significant in the former.

      Auto-correlation function (ACF)

      The ACF illustrates the relationship between the spatial variation in the distribution of roughness. It is a valuable tool for signal processing since it offers fundamental insights into the relationship between wavelength and surface amplitude features. The mathematical representation of ACF C(β) is
      C(β)=∫−∞∞z(x)z(x+β)dxRq2
      (14)
      where β is shift distance and z(x) is the amplitude distribution function (ADF). Typically, the randomness in the surface profile is described by the Gaussian/normal probability distribution function p(z) as
      p(z)=12πRqexp−z22Rq2
      (15)
      Often C(β) is forced44, 45 to fit into an exponential function and the correlation
      length ℓc is identified. ℓc is a function of the fluctuations in surface topography and is an indicator of the statistical independence of the amplitudes at two points. Figure 5 shows the variation of correlation functions for two different rough profiles along with their correlation length.

      Roughness measurement: Techniques and theory

      Surface roughness plays an important role in product quality assessment. Hence, the measurement of roughness either during manufacturing or post-manufacturing is essential before the workpiece is integrated into an assembly. Further, the machining processes influence the value of roughness.46 Depending on the mechanisms and parameters of the machining and the material of the workpiece, various types of sensors are employed to measure roughness. The conventional approach to measuring the surface topography is by caressing a physical stylus across the surface in a raster motion. These stylus-based devices are often useful for simple machining operations. Contact-based measurements are not suitable for in-situ measurements in which the workpiece is in motion or subjected to machining. Further, due to their high-resolution, non-contact measurement systems based on optical,47 electrical,48 and pneumatic49 mechanisms have gained attention.
      A brief summary of various measurement techniques is provided in Table 2. Among the non-contact techniques listed, the ones based on ultrasonics, lasers, fiber optics, and quartz crystal can be integrated into machining equipment, and in-situ measurement of the roughness is possible. On the contrary, the profilometer and microscopy methods cannot be integrated into machining equipment due to the complex shapes of the workpiece, the large size of the optics, and the high mismatch in the working environments of machining and microscopes. We now review the various mechanisms of roughness measurement.

      Profilometry

      Two broad categories exist in this measuring technique: contact (stylus) type and non-contact (optical) type. A stylus profilometer (SP) is contact-based and is widely used as a surface measurement tool due to its rapid inspection. ISO 327456 describes the characteristics and basic requirements of an SP for measuring roughness and waviness. ISO 1217957 describes the process for calibrating and adjusting the metrological characteristics of an SP as explained in ISO 3274. The tip of the stylus probe typically comprises sapphire or diamond with a tip radius of 2 µm (or 0.08 mil), 5 µm, and 10 µm and a cone taper angle of 60° or 90°. The stylus is caressed on the surface of the workpiece at a constant speed to determine the variations in surface height.58 The topographic information is obtained from a point-by-point scan of surface height along a line on the surface. The vertical resolution of SP lies between 0.1 nm and 100 µm.59 Due to the limited size of the stylus tip, the horizontal resolution is constrained; typically, it is between 0.1 µm and several micrometers. Such resolutions are acceptable for most of the topographic evaluations60, 61 used on shop floors as well as in laboratories. The times of measurement using an SP are smaller than that from most optical measurement techniques.
      The optical image of an SP is shown in Figure 6(a) and the optical profilometer in Figure 6(b). The image of a pointed stylus tip, such as the one shown in Figure 6(a), can damage the surface. Thus, SPs cannot be used for non-destructive evaluations. The limitations of SPs are: rendering of only 2D surface profiles, useful for small surface areas only, and unsuitable for in-situ measurements and internal surface evaluation.
      To overcome the limitations of SPs, optical profilometers were developed.71, 72 The measurement is based on the principle of two-beam interferometry as shown in Figure 6(c). The vertical resolution of the optical profilometer can be, typically, up to several angstroms whenever the lateral resolution is in the range of 0.3-8 µm. This technique generates the surface profile in 2D as well as in 3D. Due to their higher sensitivity and resolution, capability for large-area inspection, and faster inspection speeds than SP, optical profilometer have been widely used for industrial applications. A summary of contact type (stylus) and non-contact type (optical) profilometer to measure the surface roughness of various materials (Figure 7) subjected to different machining operations is shown in Table 3.

      Laser scanning method

      Laser and electron beams have been used to alter the surface topology75 as well as in the reconstruction of surfaces.76 The technology to use lasers in surface texturing was developed and commercialized in the years 1970–1980 at the Center for Research in Metallurgy (Cockerill Sambre, Belgium).77 Laser beams facilitate a non-destructive procedure to determine the surface roughness. Although useful for in-situ surface roughness assessment, laser profilometry78 typically needs expensive and big equipment, making it challenging to deploy. The schematic of lased-based roughness measurement is shown in Figure 8(a). The instrument comprises a laser (a coherent light source), spatial filter, a collimating lens, and another photon spatial filter. The laser beam is focused to form a spot on the workpiece using a lens. Upon projection, the minuscule irregularities scatter the beam in a diffusive manner, unlike the smooth surface which scatters specularly. These mechanisms are shown in Figure 8(b). With an increase in roughness, the specular component diminishes, and the diffusive component increases. The scattered beam is detected using a data acquisition unit and analyzed to calculate roughness. Beckmann and Spizzichino79 have used the scattering of light by Kirchhoff approximation method to estimate roughness. If the RMS roughness Rq is substantially less than the wavelength λ of the light, then the correlation between specular reflectance R and Rq is expressed as79
      RR0=exp−4πRqcosθiλ2
      (16)
      where R0 is the total reflectance from the rough surface which is determined by measuring the total light intensity dispersed in all directions along with the specular direction and θi is the angle of incidence. For a workpiece with minimum roughness, that is, a smooth surface, R0 represents the specular reflectance from the surface. The specular component of the beam diminishes with an increase in roughness, that is, if Rq ≥ λ/10, R is no longer quantifiable. If roughness-induced light-absorption processes are negligible, R0 is equal to the specular reflectance of a perfectly smooth surface of the same material. The scale of roughness up to the order of a wavelength can be identified using the relationships between surface height, and near- and far-field scattered light pattern, as described in the work by Welford.80 Lu et al.81 have demonstrated a light scattering method to measure online surface roughness with laser light illumination. The surface roughness is determined by analyzing the spatial intensity distribution of laser light scattered from the surface being examined, as shown in Figure 9. Leger et al.82 developed the speckle pattern correlation method to measure roughness. By using this technique, two speckle patterns are captured on a film by shining an unexpanded laser at a test surface at various illumination angles as shown in Figure 10. The produced film was placed in a convergent laser beam to study Young’s fringes, and the contrast of the fringes was used to calculate the surface roughness.
      Laser scanning confocal microscopy (LSCM) has also been used to determine the roughness parameters in 2D and 3D.84 The LSCM operates within the realm of light microscopy, utilizing laser light along a confocal optical path to generate images. Diverging from conventional light microscopy, where images are simultaneously formed for all observed points across the entire field of view, the LSCM employs a meticulous pixel-by-pixel imaging approach by utilization of photomultipliers, or charge-coupled devices, resulting in enhanced precision and detailed image acquisition.
      A summary of roughness measurements using laser scanning methods on various materials subjected to different machining processes is shown in Table 4. Based on the data, it is evident that lasers are suitable for the measurement of roughness in hundreds of nanometers. The lowest detected Rais 0.005 µm. The assessment of surface roughness, by principles of light scattering, has become simpler with the advancement of lasers, contemporary optics, and photodiode arrays.

      Fiber optics sensors

      The optical methods have been extensively used in industry because of their non-contact feature, high measurement speed, and cloud integration.95 Due to its small size, low cost, and tunable operation frequency, fiber optics-based probe sensing technology among other optical techniques has been used for non-contact surface roughness measurement. Interferometry,96, 97 speckle,98 and light scattering99 are the most popular optical techniques for measuring surface roughness. Phase-modulated sensors based on fiber interferometry and intensity-modulated sensors based on surface reflection are the two measuring tenets used with fiber optic sensing devices.100 By applying the interference phenomenon between two coherent light waves, Bradley et al.101 established the first optical fiber interferometer system for the assessment of surface morphology. Although interferometer systems that use fringe projection and image processing can achieve high resolution, it is not feasible to use these techniques to measure the roughness while being manufactured.102
      The block diagram of the fiber optics sensor for measuring roughness is shown in Figure 11(a). The transmitting and receiving fibers are attached to the sensing probe at opposite angles above the workpiece surface. The reflected light is received by the detector, passed to an amplifier, and converted to a digital signal by the data acquisition. The reflected light is sensitive to the distance between the surface being measured and the sensor probe’s head, as shown in Figure 11(b).
      The angles of emitting and receiving light depend on the refractive index n0 and numerical aperture (NA) of the fiber. The NA of an optical system is a measure of its angular acceptance of incident light. If the emitting and receiving fibers have the same NA, the emitting angle θe is expressed as
      θ=sin−1NAn0.
      (17)
      The reflection from the surface depends on the roughness, wavelength, angle of incidence, and the properties of surface. The theoretical framework to explain the dispersion of electromagnetic radiation from a rough surface by assuming a Gaussian distribution has been developed by Beckmann and Spizzichino.79 Equation 16 illustrates the relation between the specular reflectance R and the total reflectance Rowith the constraint that R/R0> 0.6.
      A summary on the use of optical fibers to measure surface roughness by light sources of different wavelengths and angle of incidence is provided in Table 5. Based on the data tabulated here, we conclude that fiber optics sensors with different types of light sources have been used to measure roughness in the micro and sub-micrometer regimes. Their precision levels lie in between that of lasers and ultrasonic sensors. Lasers, fiber optics, and LEDs employ using electromagnetic waves, which are governed by Maxwell’s equations. Further, the expressions for near- and far-field distances, aperture, etc. are the same as those of acoustic waves, which are discussed in the next section. This is due to the identical mathematical form of the governing equations in an isotropic medium. The theoretical aspects of optical measurements are discussed in ref.98, 108 In the microscope, the resolution is determined by the wavelength. The transverse resolution dt and
      lateral resolution dl of a laser beam are
      dt=0.61λsinθ0and dl=λ2sinθ0
      (18)

      Ultrasonics

      Ultrasonic sensors are extensively used to non-invasively determine the health of a structure, including thickness, using elastic waves of frequencies between kHz and MHz.110 As the transducers are capable of measurements in both liquids and air, the low-power transducers have emerged as one of the non-contact methods to measure roughness since the early 80’s.111 The schematic for this measurement is shown in Figure 12(a). Piezoelectric transducers are typically employed for the generation and reception of ultrasonic pulses. The signals to the transducer are fed by a function generator. As acoustic waves of high frequencies encounter the surface of a workpiece, a large portion of the waves are scattered backwards (reflection) due to the mismatch in the impedance of the workpiece and the surrounding fluid. The reflection is governed by the local surface profile, that is, roughness. The reflected waves, measured by another ultrasonic transducer, are acquired by a digital oscilloscope and computer. The scattering of an ultrasonic wave at a workpiece immersed in a liquid is schematically shown in Figure 12. Specular and diffusive reflections are observed when the profile smooth and rough, respectively. Over the past few decades, many researchers112, 113 have investigated the use of ultrasonic sensors for the measurement of roughness by immersing the workpiece in liquid techniques. Although successful, these ultrasonic immersion techniques cannot be extended for in-situ measurements in manufacturing processes due to complications in arrangement and maintenance. To overcome such difficulties, some efforts114-116 have been laid for the use of air-coupled ultrasound technique for surface roughness measurements of wood, foams, and concrete surfaces, but not for machined workpieces.
      Bui et al.115 reported the feasibility of an air-coupled ultrasonic roughness measurements technique using a broadband air-coupled capacitance transducer in pitch-catch configuration. The reflected wave from the rough surface was measured in specular configuration and a Kirchhoff-based scattering model was used to obtain the relation between the amplitude of the reflected wave and the surface roughness. It was found that the amplitude decreases significantly as roughness decreases. Birt et al.114 established the use of ultrasonic spectroscopy technique to measure the surface roughness of hidden corroded surfaces. A piezoelectric polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) transducer of spectral width 20 MHz was used to scan a surface of Rq ranging from 3.4 to 42.6 µm. Wang et al.116 have performed an extensive analysis on roughness including analytical models based on Gaussian beam theory and phased screen approximation for micro-exfoliation using ultrasonics. Recently, ultrasonic methods have also been used for in-situ monitoring in microfabrication processes such as microcellular injection molding. In the work by Zhao et al.,117 the scattering of waves on a rough surface was analyzed to examine the sensitivity of angle of incidence. Subsequently, based on Kirchhoff and phased screen approximation methods a relationship was established between attenuation coefficients and roughness.
      Lian et al.109 presented another in-situ roughness measurement technique based on the attenuation of scattered ultrasonic waves in milling and grinding. Lopez et al.120 reported the inspection of metal additive manufacturing parts using phased array ultrasonic technique. The effectiveness of this technique was demonstrated on components—manufactured using wire arc additive manufacturing—each with a different scale of roughness. A summary of roughness measurements through ultrasonic methods on various materials subjected to different machining processes is tabulated in Table 6. Based on the data presented here, it is evident that high-frequency ultrasonic techniques have been used for roughness measurements in various fabrication and machining processes.
      While the working distance of ultrasonic sensors for measurement is 4-20 cm, the same for laser-based measurements can be much larger. Further, comparing Tables 4 and 6, it is evident that the resolution of ultrasonic sensors is three orders (micrometers) lower than that of lasers (nanometers). The cases where in-situ measurements are possible are limited to the static state of the workpiece. Hence, challenges remain for the measurement of roughness in real-time machining. An ultrasonic transducer is typically a disk-shaped piezoelectric ceramic.122 A combination of piezoelectric ceramic materials—called phased arrays—is widely used to control the shape of the wavefront to achieve focused or diffusive beams. The spatial distribution of the beam comprises two main regions. The region near the transducer is referred to as the near-field or Fresnel zone. With propagation, the shape of the beam deviates and spreads into the far-field or Fraunhofer zone. The near-field distance ln, beam diameter dB, spread angle α, and lateral resolution ∆d of flat circular transducer are123
      l=D24λ=D2f4c,dB=1.02FcfD,sinα2=0.51cfD,and Δd=0.221ctpλAcosθ1
      (19)
      where D is diameter of the element, λ = c/f is wavelength, f is frequency, c is phase speed in the medium, F is focal length, tp is time taken to complete the path, A is the aperture length, and θi is angle of incidence of beam.

      Quartz crystal microbalance

      Quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) is typically a ∼ 1-cm-diameter circular disk-like device that operates based on its resonant frequency.124 It works on the piezoelectric nature to monitor the resonance frequency of the crystal as well as the dissipation of the energy of oscillations. A QCM is highly sensitive to change in mass — 1 nanogram — accrued on or recurred from the surface. The breakthrough for the use of QCMs as delicate mass balances was achieved by Sauerbrey125 in 1959. The schematic of QCM configuration is shown in Figure 13. Both the workpiece and the quartz crystal act as electrodes. Sauerbrey demonstrated that the change in frequency ∆f of the
      Δf=−2f02AρuΔm
      (20)
      where A is the interfacial area between quartz crystal and the workpiece, ρ is the mass density of quartz, µ is the shear modulus of quartz, and f0 is frequency of oscillation of the pure quartz crystal. Many investigations126, 127 successfully demonstrated the response of the QCM to the change in surface roughness, both theoretically and experimentally. Daikhin and Urbakh128-130 have done extensive research on the frequency and dissipation response of a rough and viscously laden QCM. The regime is considered as slight rough if |δz| << 1 and Rq/δN << 1.
      McHale et al.131 have provided a detailed analysis accounting for the shifts in frequency and the dissipation factor. These are given as132
      𝓁𝓁𝓁𝓁Δf=−δNf2ρρqμq1+RQ2lc2FlcδNandΔD=2δNf2ρρqμq1+RQ2lc2ϕlcδN
      (21)
      where f represents the resonance frequency, ρq is mass density and µqis the shear modulus of quartz resonator, and F and ϕ are the scaling functions, respectively. Rechendorff et al.133 investigated the effect of roughness on a titanium-coated substrate on frequency and dissipation responses of quartz resonator in a sucrose solution. A correlation between the shift in frequency and measured surface roughness was observed. Subsequently, it was revealed that the shift in the dissipation factor is unaffected by an increasing the roughness. Shakti et al.134 have investigated the effect on roughness due to deposition of polystyrene in a spin coated method on to a QCM sensor. They reported that there was no significant change in electrical impedance of the quartz crystal resonator. In Djoko et al.,135 the effect of different solvent on morphology of polystyrene and stearic acid layer by using QCM has been investigated. The polystyrene layer was coated on the top of the QCM sensor by using the spin coating method and stearic acid coating by using the vacuum evaporation method with chloroform and toluene solvent. QCMs typically have sensitivities ranging from picograms to nanograms. The resolution of QCM is often in the range of sub-nanogram. Advanced QCM instruments and signal processing techniques can further enhance the resolution.

      Scanning tunneling microscope (STM)

      To characterize the surface at the nanometer level, generally two techniques are used, namely STM and atomic force microscopy (AFM). These techniques are utilized to obtain fine details at a sub-nanometric scale on the surface of a workpiece. The tunneling microscopy was first introduced by G. Binning in 1983136 by applying it to superconductor materials. It was then expanded to surface topography by using inelastic tunneling spectroscopy.137 It can detect surface features in the range of 0.1 nm with a depth resolution of 0.01 nm through an extremely sharp conductive tip.138 Typically, this technique is used as a sandwich configuration of metal insulator-metal or semiconductor. The electrons that already exist in the workpiece are utilized as the source of radiation. The STM works on the principle of quantum tunneling. The schematic of STM is shown in Figure 14. It consists of a metallic tip connected with a piezoelectric scanner that acts as one electrode; the workpiece is the other electrode). As the tip is brought near the surface, a bias voltage ensures that current flows through the vacuum tunnel. This tunneling current I is proportional to the width of the gap d and applied voltage VT as136
      I∝VTexp−Aϕ1/2d
      (22)
      where ϕ is the work function (the average tunnel height). Yang and Talke139 have also utilized the STM to measure the roughness of thin-film magnetic recording disks. Garcia et al.140 have revealed a model to study the roughness using an STM, operated at atmospheric pressure. They have introduced two parameters to characterize surface areas in the micrometer and sub-micrometer range, which are termed granular roughness and micro-roughness. The resolution of STM is typically 1 nm, corresponding to a change in barrier height.141

      Atomic force microscopy

      STM requires the workpiece to be electrically conductive. To overcome this constraint, Binning et al.143 introduced the atomic force microscope (AFM) in 1986, which works on the combined principles of STM and SP. The schematic of this setup is shown in Figure 15. In this technique, the force between the probe and workpiece is detected rather than the tunneling current as in STM. The probe is attached to a flexible cantilever and the workpiece is mounted on a piezoelectric scanner. The surface is scanned with a sharp probe and the interaction force between the tip and workpiece is detected. A laser beam is impinged on the cantilever also referred to as the probe. When the cantilever deflects under loading, the photodiode detects the angular deflection of the reflected beam. The changes in the magnitude of deflection are responsible for the interaction force between the tip and surface. The spatial variations in the measured force correspond to the variations in surface irregularities.
      The typical deflections are ±0.02 nm, forces are 0.2 nN, and lever force constants are 10 N/m. An AFM unit can operate in two different modes: contact and dynamic. In contact mode AFM, the tip raster scans over the surface and obtains the topographic images of spatial resolution as low as 0.01 nm, lateral resolution ∼ 0.2 nm, and a sensitivity of 0.01 nm.

      Modeling and simulation of rough surfaces

      Instruments have different resolutions, sensitivities, and levels of precision. Hence, the accuracies of roughness parameters explained in the second section are dependent on the instrument used.144 It is critical to characterize the rough surface using intrinsic parameters that appropriately convey spatial information and are also independent of scan size. Therefore, to know the deviations from the actual profile of the surface, geometric models were developed.145 Mathematically, the amplitude densities of roughness are expressed using distribution functions like Gaussian, Bessel, power law, Lorentzian, etc.146, 147, 148 or a power spectrum.149 Several kinds of attempts were made to predict roughness. For example, analytical and finite element method-based models for finishing processes such as AFF150, 151, 152 and magnetorheological-AFF153, 154; regression models for hard turning155; and artificial neural network (ANN) models for electro-discharge diamond grinding156 were developed. Further, the uniformness of profiles, either measured or modeled, is quantified in terms of the ACF,157, 158 given by Equation 14. In this section, we present a summary of the various models used for the geometric description of surface roughness.

      Mandelbrot–Weierstrass function model

      Let us suppose a 3D surface profile z(x,y) as shown in Figure 2, has several peaks and heights with mechanical properties such as continuous, non-differentiable, and statistically self-affine.
      Majumdar and Bhushan159 have revealed that the Weierstrass-Mandelbrot (WM) function satisfies all these properties. A fractal-based model on the WM function to represent the 2D surface profile is expressed as
      z(x)=GDm−1Σn=n2∞cos2πγnx+ϕnγ2−Dmnwithγ>1and 1<Dm<1
      (23)
      where Dm represents the fractal dimension,160G is characteristic length scale γn are the frequency modes, ϕn and ψn are the phases corresponding to different frequency modes. The phases have been normalized by considering a non-integer γ. Extending the same, Majunder and Tien161 have developed the function to represent the surface profile in 3D form as
      z(x,y)=GDm−1Σn=n1nmaxcos2πγnx+ϕ1cos2πγny+ϕnγ2−Dmn
      (24)
      Subsequently, Lai et al.162 have also quantitatively described the surface roughness at the microscopic level using the fractal dimension parameter.

      Random midpoint displacement model

      A major drawback of the WM model is that it does not produce an isotropic spectrum. To overcome this drawback, the random midpoint displacement model has been developed. It utilizes the diamond-square algorithm163 to generate random profiles. To analyze the random surface, it is a very critical numerical instrument that generates the same morphological data arrays as most of the scanning acquisition methods generate for real-range images. Seo et al.164 have used the random displacement method to generate and quantify the rough surface.

      Phenomenological model

      This model is utilized for modeling of surface roughness of microwave applications.165, 166 Hammerstad and Jensen167 and Groiss et al.168 have revealed that the high-frequency current follows the surface profile and results in current indirection. In such models, the correction factors KHJ and KG have been derived from measuring the additional losses in current due to the roughness:
      KHJ=1+2πtan−11.4Rqδs2and KG=1+exp−δs2Rq1.6
      (25)
      where δs is the skin depth. The major drawback of these types of models is that they are suited for low roughness or low frequency only, as they saturate when the correction factors reach 2. Whereas, in the work of Horn et al.,169 it has been experimentally proved that the losses for rough surfaces easily exceed twice the losses for smooth surfaces calculated using the skin effect.

      Artificial neural networks

      The rough surface can be modeled using ANNs.170, 171 In some applications like integrated circuit technology, it is crucial to understand how process parameters affect surface roughness. However, controlling the process parameters using classical modeling methods becomes challenging. Consequently, ANNs are used to model the rough surfaces to integrate the process parameters.172 A single node layer along with hidden and output layers was chosen as shown in Figure 16(a). The algorithm is utilized to assist the network in acquiring the necessary weights for generating the surface with appropriate roughness parameters. The weights are updated until the calculated roughness parameters match with the predefined error margin. The weights wij are updated as ∆wij = αeϵ/2, where e is the input parameter, α represents the learning factor, and ϵ represents the difference between desired and calculated value of Rq . Even though the feed-forward network, shown in Figure 16(a), is utilized to quantify the electrical parameters like capacitance and electric field variation as well as for modeling, it is not well suited for understanding the effect of processing parameters. Consequently, the backpropagation algorithm174 is used to understand the effect of process parameters on roughness by using neural networks. The topology of the feed forward-back propagation is shown in Figure 16(b) which maps the process parameters to the roughness parameters. The input layer of the network consists of multiple inputs that represent the process parameters like voltage, current, feed force, temperature etc. To update the weights, standard least square and gradient descent learning methods are used, and all the weights are updated by the following relation: ∆wij(n) = β∆wij(n − 1) + ηδj(n)yi(n) where β represents the positive momentum constant, δj the local gradient, η the learning rate, and yi is the input signal. Initially, the network is tested for arbitrary input parameters and surfaces having different roughness are created.
      To simulate and control the process parameters for random rough surfaces, many other models have been introduced. Guvenc et al.175 have developed the neuro-based fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) model to estimate the surface roughness (Ra) and tool vibrations (Acc) of AA6013 aluminum alloy during dry turning. Ding et al.176, 177 have model the random rough surface by considering the ACF and power spectral density function in their work. Suresh et al.178 have developed a surface roughness model using a genetic algorithmic approach called response surface methodology (RSM) for machining mild steel workpieces.

      Fast Fourier transform (FFT)

      The Fourier transform of the waveform represents the decomposition of the surface profile to a summation of spatial harmonic functions.179, 180, 181 Additionally, this function is suitable for simulating the rough surface in 3D182 using
      zxj,yk=Σj=1mΣk=1nSj,kexp2πiϕj,k+jxm+kyn
      (26)
      where ϕj,k is the random phase angle, j and k are integers. The spectral density Sj,k represents is calculated as
      Sj,k=1mnΣp=1mΣq=1nCpqexp−2πijpm+kqn
      (27)
      where Cpq represents an ACF.

      Challenges for roughness measurements and Industry 4.0

      Similar to various machining processes leading to different levels of roughness, the instruments used to measure the corresponding roughness are also different. Conventionally, roughness has always been measured only after removing the workpieces from the machine. In recent years, efforts have been made to measure the dimensions and roughness while the workpiece is being machined.183, 184 In-situ methods are useful in avoiding polishing or machining the workpiece in multiple stages, over-polishing, and efforts to reposition the workpiece in the last orientation.
      Such methods save power, time, cost, and material. Furthermore, in-situ methods not only help in monitoring a machining process, but also help in integrating various machines and processes, automation, and monitoring. All these efforts are part of the standards of Industry 4.0,185 which prescribe that all processes must be automated and parameters must be continuously monitored for efficient and sustainable use.
      Manufacturing must always contend with growing consumer demands for higher product quality, more product variety, low costs, and increased global competitiveness.186, 187 The implementation of reliable and robust monitoring systems is crucial for semi-automatic and automatic machining systems. In this line, the main challenge in achieving the desired roughness and tolerance is that the machining is not performed in one stage. The workpiece is machined, removed from the machine, measured for dimensional tolerances and roughness, and then positioned back in the workpiece holder for further machining. Due to this sequence, the workpiece is invariably oriented differently compared to its position in the first sequence. This makes repeatability an issue. In traditional manufacturing, parts are produced in masses, after ensuring correctness by measurements on the first few parts. In today’s manufacturing, parts require tight tolerances and are made in batches. Hence, measurements are made more often leading to an increase in production time. To overcome these challenges of consistency and accuracy, we envision the development of the following:
      Portable devices for in-situ measurement: These should scan the surface profile of the workpiece while they are held in the machine, thereby saving time.
      Multisensor measurement: As evident from the literature survey, every method of measurement is specific to a set of machining processes. To ensure the reliability of measurements, increased confidence in the data, and full surface reconstruction, measurements from multiple sensors are desired. Some efforts are already in place to make optical measurements188 including three-dimensional surface reconstruction,189 toward fitting in the goals of industry 4.0. Non-contact measurements such as air-coupled ultrasonic sensors, laser scanners, and optical systems are essential in smart factories.
      Calibration: The sensors need to be calibrated based on (a) the line and form features of the complex geometry; (b) the medium of the environment; and (c) the nano, micro, meso, or macroscale of the roughness.
      Cloud-based analytics: Development of filters and data fusion methodologies190 for the data measured from different sensors. A comprehensive integration of measurements using advanced precision sensors, signal processing systems, physics-based simulations, statistical methods such as ANNs, and machine learning algorithms to predict the roughness and suggest amendments is needed. To establish the cloud-based analytics for fitting in the objectives of Industry 4.0 to predict the surface quality, various equipment must be installed, as shown in Figure 17.
      Digital twinning and virtual reality191: The advancement in measurements, processing, and simulation can lead to prediction as well as corrections in the process parameters. This can be facilitated by the development of digital twins. Further, as Industry 4.0 aspires to transform the interplay between humans and technology radically with advances in smart manufacturing technologies, we believe the visualization of data in multiple ways can help in decision-making. Similar to the projected topographies of the surface as colormaps, profiles, and tables on computer screens, the development of IoT to generate scanned surface and deviation plots in real-time by augmented reality (AR) would be useful. Such methods would help in understanding the variations in roughness directly in the production environment. AR headsets or smart glasses would let the operators and maintenance workers see virtual overlays of surface roughness data on real things, enabling faster decision-making during production.
      Miscellaneous: Strategic methods must be established for sophisticated cases: very large areas comprising small features, freeform surfaces, porous and multi-material.

      Conclusions

      Different manufacturing processes generate different surface characteristics requiring different parameters such as average, root-mean-squared, skewness, kurtosis, etc. for surface topography. Each of these parameters specifies a particular characteristic of the machined surface. Starting with the definitions of these parameters, their importance was discussed. The deliberation on the non-contact and contact sensors for roughness measurement of profiles generated by various machining processes leading to the different regimes of roughness was performed. For the quantification of roughness at the nanometric scale, non-contact measurement techniques are suitable because of their high resolution and sensitivity. The theoretical limits of focal length, range, and resolution using elastic and electromagnetic waves, which are the basis of a majority of sensors, were detailed. Thereafter, we summarized the mathematical models of roughness and their importance. In the end, we proposed ways for measuring roughness toward fitting in the scheme of Industry 4.0.
